Deceitful describes someone or something that deliberately creates a false impression in another person's mind. The key word here is deliberately — deceitful is never about accidents or innocent mistakes. It always involves a choice to mislead.

When you call someone deceitful, you are saying: this person intentionally makes others believe things that are not true. It is one of the strongest negative things you can say about someone's character.

Think of it in three parts:

1. There is a truth.
2. The deceitful person knows that truth.
3. They actively hide it, twist it, or replace it with a lie — on purpose.

So a deceitful person is not confused or mistaken. They know exactly what they are doing. They are being strategically dishonest.

The word can describe several things:

A person. This is the most common use. A deceitful person has a habit or tendency of misleading others. It describes their character, not just one act. Calling someone deceitful suggests this is who they are, not just something they did once.

"She seemed kind and generous, but over time I realized she was deeply deceitful — everything she said had a hidden agenda."

Behaviour, actions, or tactics. The things a person does can be deceitful even if the person themselves might not always be.

"The salesman used deceitful tactics, making the product sound far better than it actually was."

Words, promises, or appearances. Even a smile, a tone of voice, or an outward appearance can be deceitful if it is designed to mislead.

"His calm, reassuring words were deceitful — he knew the company was about to collapse."

Deceitful carries a sharp moral judgment. When you use this word, you are not just describing what someone did — you are condemning it. It implies a betrayal of trust, because the person being deceived is trusting the other person to be honest, and that trust is being exploited.

This is why being called deceitful feels like a serious accusation. It goes beyond a single lie. It suggests a pattern, a nature, an intent to manipulate.
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Dishonest is the broader, more general word. A dishonest person might lie, cheat, or steal. Deceitful is more specific — it focuses on creating false impressions, on making people believe something untrue.

Deceptive is the closest synonym to deceitful, but there is a subtle difference. Deceptive can describe things that mislead you without any human intention behind it — like a deceptive road that looks short but is actually very long. Deceitful almost always implies a person's deliberate intent. A person can be deceitful; a winding road is deceptive.

Misleading is weaker and softer. Something misleading might cause you to reach the wrong conclusion, but it might not be on purpose. Deceitful always involves purpose.

Fraudulent involves deception that breaks the law, usually for money or legal gain. All fraudulent behaviour is deceitful, but not all deceitful behaviour is fraudulent.

Duplicitous is very close in meaning — it specifically means saying one thing while secretly doing or believing another, like a two-faced person. Deceitful is the broader term; duplicitous emphasises the double-faced quality.

Untruthful simply means not telling the truth. It is milder and does not necessarily suggest cunning or a pattern. Deceitful implies more cleverness and deliberateness.

• "The deceitful politician promised better roads and hospitals during the campaign, knowing he had no intention of delivering either."
  • "I trusted him completely, so it was painful to discover how deceitful he had been all along."
  • "The advertisement was deceitful, showing results that almost no real customer ever achieved."
  • "A deceitful smile played on her lips as she told him everything was perfectly fine."
  • "Children are often taught early that being deceitful may work in the short term, but it destroys trust in the long run."

Once you know deceitful, the related words come naturally:

  • Deceit (noun) — the act or practice of deceiving. "His entire friendship with her was built on deceit."
  • Deceitfully (adverb) — in a deceitful manner. "She smiled deceitfully and said she had no idea what happened."
  • Deceitfulness (noun) — the quality or state of being deceitful. "His deceitfulness eventually cost him all his friends."
  • Deceive (verb) — to make someone believe something false. "He deceived everyone around him for years."
  • Deception (noun) — the act of deceiving, or a trick used to deceive. "The whole story was an elaborate deception."

The opposites of deceitful help you understand it even more clearly:

Honest, truthful, sincere, straightforward, transparent, frank, candid, trustworthy.

A person who is the opposite of deceitful tells you what they truly think and feel, does not hide their real intentions, and can be trusted to mean what they say.

Deceitful means deliberately causing others to believe something false — and it always implies intent, cunning, and a betrayal of trust. It is one of the strongest ways to say that a person or their actions cannot be trusted.
